Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

U1 · Introduction to creativity

Creativity is work you can pace: open many options, then choose what fits the brief — not a talent myth.

Open many doors on Monday; close most of them on Tuesday — that rhythm is the craft, not the mood.

(Tao of Creativity)

Analysis opens the class

Sessions 1–2: the professor shows how to analyse. From session 3: two students start with a 15-minute defence each.

The professor models first; from session three, you defend what the piece is made of.

(Tao of Creativity)

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

How to analyse (model)

Say what the piece is made of first: language, medium, support. Then ask where meaning travels when someone else sees it.

Name language, medium, and support before you praise the idea — otherwise you are judging a shadow.

(Tao of Creativity)

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

1 · Open, then close

First invent many possibilities. Then pick what fits the needs of the brief — one creative act can hold both moves.

The same creative act may involve both divergent and convergent thinking.

(Craft 2000, 30)

Image: Chalk drawing by Michelangelo: a large, carefully modelled study of a bent leg and torso, with two small quick sketches of a seated figure in the corners.

Studies for the Libyan Sibyl · Michelangelo Buonarroti · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • First we open: invent many options. That is divergent thinking.
  • Then we close: pick what fits the needs of the brief. That is convergent thinking.
  • One creative job often needs both moves.

Source: the quote and the open/close distinction (divergent; convergent = possibilities that fit a set of needs) are (Craft 2000, 30). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Think of your last project. Where did you open, and where did you close?

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

2 · Four skills tests measure

Fluency (many ideas), flexibility (many angles), originality (ideas few other people have), elaboration (work the details). Many workshops try to raise these scores.

Fluency - the ability to produce a large number of ideas or solutions to a problem rapidly.

(Chen 2011, 26)

Course diagram · Koch triangle · #5cc4358a9bdb · Original course SVG

  • Guilford's four abilities, as summarised by Chen, give us shared words: fluency (many ideas quickly), flexibility (several different approaches at the same time), originality (ideas few other people produce), elaboration (work the details).
  • Many workshops try to raise these scores.
  • A higher score is not the same as a better idea in a real brief. That is the next slide.

Source: the four abilities and the Fluency quote are (Chen 2011, 26); fluency, flexibility, originality as what "most workshops try to enhance" is (Csikszentmihalyi 1996, chap. 3). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Which of the four skills do you use most? Which one do you avoid?

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

3 · Tests are not the whole story

Scoring well on “uses of a brick” does not prove you are strong in another field — tests need context.

After all, the ability of divergent thinking with a paper clip may tell us little about an individual's talent in music.

(Chen 2011, 26)

Image: An 1893 newspaper advertisement for the Gem paper clip: a large line drawing of the double-loop wire clip beside text praising it for holding papers together.

Gem paper clip advertisement, January 1893 · Unknown advertiser (1893) · Public domain · Source

  • Scoring high on "how many uses for a brick or a paper clip" is not the same as judgement inside a real brief.
  • A test in one field may tell us little about talent in another, such as music.

Source: the paper-clip/music quote is (Chen 2011, 26). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: What would a test of design judgement need to include?

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

4 · Name the problem first

Before you grab a creativity technique, say what is unclear in the brief — name the problem, then pick the tool.

Before you pick a method, write the question the brief still refuses to answer.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: Rodin's bronze The Thinker: a seated nude man leans forward, chin resting on his hand, absorbed in thought before acting.

The Thinker · Auguste Rodin (sculpture); Cleveland Museum of Art (photograph, CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Before you pick a creativity technique, say what is fuzzy in the brief.
  • Tools help after the problem is framed.
  • Problems are not given; they are built from an unclear situation, and how you state one already points to an answer.

Source: the slide quote is a Tao of Creativity line; the lesson cites (Schön 1983, 40), (Buchanan 1992, 16) and (Csikszentmihalyi 1996, chap. 4) for the third bullet: problems are constructed from uncertain situations (Schön), every formulation of a wicked problem corresponds to a formulation of a solution (Buchanan), presented vs discovered problems (Csikszentmihalyi). Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: What question does your current brief still refuse to answer?

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

5 · Techniques are tools, not scripts

A method helps you talk with the situation. It does not replace your judgement or the brief.

A technique is a lever, not a verdict — it moves the work; it does not replace your judgement.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: An 18th-century pocket set of drawing instruments by Peter Dollond: a ruler, a scale and four brass and steel instruments laid out beside their open shagreen case.

Pocket set of drawing instruments · Peter Dollond (instrument maker); The Metropolitan Museum of Art (photograph, CC0) · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • A method helps you talk with the situation.
  • It does not replace your judgement.
  • Reflecting while you act means you are not bound by established technique.

Source: the slide quote is a Tao of Creativity line; the third bullet is (Schön 1983, 68): in reflection-in-action the practitioner "is not dependent on the categories of established theory and technique". Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: When did a method push you to a choice you would not defend?

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

6 · “Design thinking” is debated

Use useful tools — and ask when buzzwords hide weak craft or skip the hard part.

When the buzzword arrives, ask what craft it is hiding — slogans are often empty handles.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: A promotional wall covered in coloured sticky notes in vertical stripes around a screen reading 'Post-it Teamwork Tools', with product baskets on the counter below.

Post-It Notes Wall at the Fast Company Innovation Festival · Nan Palmero · CC BY 2.0 · Source

  • Use tools that help.
  • Also ask when managerial buzzwords empty out craft.
  • Offered for debate, not as settled fact: critics argue the claims for design thinking are overstated.

Source: the slide quote is a Tao of Creativity line; the third bullet is (Kimbell 2011, 285): "several issues that undermine the claims made for design thinking". Other bullets are course wording.

Ask: Name one design buzzword. What craft might it hide?

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

Recall check

Alone, from memory, 3 minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. Most definitions of creativity ask for which two things?
  2. Name the three parts of Csikszentmihalyi's system.
  3. Name the four skills that creativity tests measure.
  4. What does Chen warn about a high alternative-uses score?
  5. For Schön, where do problems in practice come from?

Course geometric background · threshold · #7a624a21 · Original course SVG

  • Timer: 3 minutes. Students answer alone, from memory, on paper; no notes, no slides.
  • Then 2 minutes in pairs: compare answers, then check the lesson.
  • Practice only: nothing is collected or graded. Five more questions with answers are on the unit's practice quiz page.

Answers:

  • 1. Something new and something that matters: novelty plus value or meaningfulness (Beghetto and Karwowski 2025, 3).
  • 2. Domain, field and person (Csikszentmihalyi 1996, chap. 2).
  • 3. Fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration (Chen 2011, 26).
  • 4. Divergent thinking with a paper clip may tell us little about talent in another field, such as music (Chen 2011, 26).
  • 5. Not as givens: they are constructed from situations that are puzzling, troubling and uncertain (Schön 1983, 40).

Ask: Which answer could you not recall? Re-read that idea before the Lab.

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

Exercise 1 · Alternative uses, scored on four skills

List as many uses for one everyday object as you can in 3 minutes, alone and in silence. Then score your list: how many uses, how many kinds, rare uses, detail.

Practises Masterclass 2–3: the four skills, and why a score is not the whole designer.

Save your list, the four scores and one sentence on your least obvious use.

Image: Alfred Stieglitz's 1917 photograph of Duchamp's Fountain: a white porcelain urinal turned on its back on a plinth, signed 'R. Mutt 1917', with an entry tag hanging from it.

Fountain · Alfred Stieglitz (photograph) / Marcel Duchamp (readymade) · Rights under review · Source

  • Timer: 3 minutes of silent listing (the slide timer). Whole exercise about 15 minutes.
  • Show one everyday object or a photo (a brick, a paper clip, a shoe). Everyone lists uses alone and in silence.
  • Fluency: count the uses. Flexibility: group them into kinds and count the kinds.
  • Originality: post every list on a shared board, or compare lists within table groups of 5–6; mark each use nobody else wrote. Reading every list aloud does not fit the time.
  • Elaboration: pick one marked use and add three concrete details.
  • Close: which shift between kinds gave your least obvious use? Treat the numbers as practice, not a talent verdict.

Source: tests like Alternate Uses ask for as many uses of a common object as possible, and the four abilities (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) are as reported in (Chen 2011, 26); the caution that such scores may say little about talent in a specific field is the same page. The steps and the shared-board scoring are course wording.

Ask: Was your rarest use also your best one?

Creativity Techniques · U1 Introduction

Exercise 2 · Cut-up and readymade: open, then close

Cut a real brief into words and draw them from an envelope. Then give an ordinary object a new title or place without changing it. Mark which moves opened options and which closed them.

Practises Masterclass 1 (open, then close) and the language / medium / support analysis.

Save the cut-up page, the readymade title and label, and your list of opening and closing moves.

Image: The 1922 Kleine Dada Soirée poster: words in German, Dutch and French, in many sizes, typefaces and directions, jumbled around giant red letters spelling 'DADA'.

Kleine Dada Soirée (Small Dada Evening) · Theo van Doesburg and Kurt Schwitters · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Timer: 25 minutes — about 12 for the cut-up, 8 for the readymade, 5 for naming the moves. Pairs.
  • Cut-up: cut the brief text into single words or short phrases; draw them one at a time; copy them in the order drawn; underline any phrase that suggests an idea and write the idea.
  • Readymade: do not change the object; change only its title, place or position. Write a title and a one-line label; show it to another pair and ask what they now see.
  • Analysis: did the change work through the language (title, label), the medium (where it is shown) or the support (the object)?
  • Name the moves: opening (cutting, drawing, re-placing) or closing (underlining, choosing a title).
  • A digital word shuffle can replace scissors.

Source: classroom adaptation in course wording; no reading-list source is cited for these two procedures yet.

Ask: Which single change did the most work, and was it an opening or a closing move?

Carry one question into next week: what is creativity for you — and what would change your answer?
